In addition to the FSR’s warning about tighter financial conditions and market liquidity strains, the Senior Loan Officer Opinion Survey points to a clear, broad-based tightening in bank credit that amplifies downside risks from the FOMC’s November 2022 rate hike and balance sheet runoff. Banks reported tighter standards across C&I lending (including foreign banks) and CRE (construction, nonfarm nonresidential, multifamily), as well as tighter terms for consumer credit—especially credit cards and residential mortgages (with lower approval likelihood for 620/680 FICO and more favorable for 720). Loan demand weakened across large, middle-market, and small firms, with softer demand for auto and credit card loans, while overall consumer loan demand was little changed and HELOC demand was stronger. Banks cited the economic outlook as a key reason for tightening and assessed higher recession risk.

Taken together, SLOOS indicates that credit supply is contracting while loan demand is softening, reinforcing restrictive financial conditions beyond policy rates and heightening growth risks. This corroborates and deepens the negative skew already flagged by the FSR, despite still-robust bank capital and liquidity. Accordingly, the overall assessment of the November 2022 policy stance and outlook turns more negative than previously indicated.
